At the moment of hatching, these altricial chicks weigh a mere 4.2 grams [Ww0 = 4.2 grams], a value consistent with the small initial masses typical of many tropical passerines. This minimal body mass at birth underscores the considerable parental investment required during the subsequent nestling phase. Field measurements indicate that the incubation temperature is pivotal for synchronizing hatching and ensuring the proper allocation of yolk reserves. Once hatched, the nestlings are entirely dependent on both parents for brooding and provisioning. Their rapid growth trajectory is fueled by a diet of insects and other arthropods delivered frequently throughout the day. The initial wet weight of 4.2 grams [Ww0 = 4.2 grams] represents a baseline from which the chicks must nearly triple their mass before they are ready to fledge, highlighting the intensive energy demands of the nestling period.

This longevity estimate, derived from mark-recapture studies in the Andean cloud forest, is notable among small neotropical warblers and suggests a life-history strategy that balances moderate annual mortality with extended reproductive opportunities. The combination of a high metabolic rate and a comparatively long lifespan presents an interesting physiological paradox for comparative life-history research.

At the 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] body temperature typical of active birds, the age at which a fledgling achieves independent flight and leaves the nest is 12 days after hatching [tx = 12 days after hatching]. The young, still dependent on parental feeding for a short period after leaving the nest, soon transition to a juvenile stage where they begin to forage on their own.
